extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO (particularly trademark practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing how practitioners must sign, certify, supervise, and present trademark and related papers to the USPTO, and the disciplinary consequences for violating those rules. Covers signature format, required certifications, supervision of non-practitioners, duties of candor and diligence, and sanctions/monitoring following misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants or registrants must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule intended to (a) increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, (b) improve accuracy of trademark submissions, and (c) safeguard integrity of the U.S. trademark register. Practitioners serving as the U.S. counsel must be authorized to practice in the U.S. and act as attorney of record for foreign-domiciled clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; an electronic signature must be personally entered by the signatory and placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP §611.01(c) elaborates: the person identified as the signatory must personally sign the printed form or personally enter the electronic signature (directly on TEAS form or in emailed form). Another person (paralegal, assistant, secretary, foreign non-U.S. attorney, etc.) may not sign or enter the name of a qualified U.S. attorney or other authorized signatory. Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature. Electronic signature must be the signatory personally entering any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as signature and placed between slashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications required when presenting papers to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner certifies whenever presenting (signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating) any trademark or patent paper to the USPTO that: (1) statements made on the practitioner's own knowledge are true; (2) statements made on information and belief are believed to be true; and that, after a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances, (i) the paper is not being presented for any improper purpose, (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by nonfrivolous argument to change law, (iii) factual allegations have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable investigation, and (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must form their knowledge/information/belief after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances. Violations of these certification requirements may jeopardize the probative value of the filing and can subject the practitioner to disciplinary action under the Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to conduct a reasonable inquiry supporting factual assertions (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before certifying factual assertions in papers presented to the USPTO, the practitioner must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports those assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule requires that factual contentions have evidentiary support or be likely to have support after reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry can form the basis for professional discipline and undermines the evidentiary weight of the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of improperly signed or false filings (void registrations / criminal & disciplinary exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a signature on a trademark application or submission fails to comply with signature rules because entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the submission is improperly executed, normally renders the application void, and a resulting registration may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False statements in trademark applications are subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001. In addition to criminal exposure, violations can lead to disciplinary action (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(d)) and case law shows applications/registrations may be invalidated (e.g., In re Cowan; In re Dermahose; In re Yusha Zhang). Improperly signed filings negatively affect the integrity of the federal trademark registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing clients; failure includes not timely informing clients of adverse consequences and not taking reasonable steps to ensure filings comply with USPTO signature rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failing this duty: not timely notifying clients of actual or potential adverse consequences to their intellectual property rights due to impermissible signing; presenting trademark documents not signed by the named signatory; not conducting reasonable inquiry as required by §11.18; failing to ensure filings were reviewed and filed in accordance with signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) and (a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must be candid toward the tribunal (the USPTO); knowingly presenting trademark documents, including sworn declarations, that were not signed by the named signatory or falsely certifying under § 11.18 violates candor obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific misconduct: knowingly presenting unsigned or improperly signed documents and certifying that factual assertions (including that the named signatory signed the document) are true when the practitioner knew they were not. Such conduct is grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities over non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are responsible for non-practitioner assistants and may not allow non-practitioner assistants to sign the practitioner's name to trademark documents presented to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule imposes supervisory obligations; allowing non-practitioner assistants (including foreign attorneys not licensed in the U.S.) to electronically enter the practitioner's signature violates this duty. Practitioners must take reasonable steps to ensure non-practitioner staff do not perform acts that require practitioner signature or create false certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct involving misrepresentation, including presenting trademark documents or sworn declarations not signed by the named signatory or allowing false certifications under § 11.18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentation includes knowingly submitting documents with false signatures or certifications. Such conduct may be charged under § 11.804(c) and supports disciplinary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the USPTO trademark registration system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the USPTO trademark registration system, including knowingly presenting improperly signed documents and allowing false certifications that the named signatory signed submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule addresses actions that undermine the registry's integrity; repeated or systemic violations (e.g., signing practices leading to many improperly executed filings) can be an aggravating factor in discipline and may prompt further corrective or disciplinary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, restrictions, and reinstatement requirements following misconduct (OED/Final Order remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary remedies can include suspension from practice before the USPTO (e.g., 30 days), limited practice during suspension (only concluding pending matters), probationary periods after suspension, requirement to complete USPTO training modules (Trademark Basics Boot Camp) prior to reinstatement, compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58, deactivation/disablement of USPTO.gov accounts, and prohibitions on obtaining or sponsoring USPTO accounts until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order may specify: suspension commencement and length, limitation to concluding client work during suspension, that a petition for reinstatement must include evidence of completed training modules, respondent must comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 and 11.60, USPTO may disable accounts, and respondent is barred from opening/verifying/sponsoring USPTO.gov accounts until reinstated. Failure to comply during probation may trigger an Order to Show Cause and potential additional suspension (up to six months) and other disciplinary steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation monitoring and reporting obligations (search/report/notify requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: While on probation, a practitioner must perform monthly searches of the USPTO online trademark search system for applications identifying them as attorney of record and promptly notify the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of any trademark filing made without their knowledge or consent; additionally, submit bi-monthly written reports to the OED Director confirming the searches and any required correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting obligations: monthly searches (tmsearch.uspto.gov) and bi-monthly written reports stating either (i) no unauthorized filings were identified, or (ii) copies of correspondence sent to the Office of Trademark Examination Policy regarding unauthorized filings. Failure to comply may lead to further action under the Final Order (Order to Show Cause, additional suspension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Client notification procedures for foreign-domiciled clients under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58(c)(3)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy 37 C.F.R. § 11.58(c)(3)(i) for foreign-domiciled clients with immediate or prospective business before the Office, a suspended practitioner may email, in the client's native language, the requisite § 11.58 notices and information (including a correctly translated copy of the Final Order) to specified email addresses under conditions that ensure the client receives the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable delivery options: (1) email to the client's email address of record (if reasonably believed to be directly accessible by the client); (2) email to any email address belonging to the client that the practitioner reasonably believes the client has direct access to; or (3) email to the foreign-domiciled third person/entity who referred the matter only if (A) practitioner takes reasonable measures to ensure the referrer promptly forwards the email with the translated Final Order and practitioner is copied, (B) practitioner takes reasonable measures to learn the client actually received the forwarded email, and (C) practitioner's affidavit submitted under § 11.58(d) describes these measures. These steps are required to comply with notification and affidavit requirements and to demonstrate reasonable measures were taken.
